title: eMudhra intermediate CA compromise
author: galadran
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores.

Root programs are run by operating system and browser vendors to vet certificate authorities and decide which ones their products trust. Trust stores are the lists of trusted root certificates that operating systems, browsers, language runtimes, libraries and applications use to verify certificates, and many are based on the root programs' lists.

comments.author: eqvinox
comments.textRawHtml:
Since I haven't seen this mentioned enough yet:

The private key for all 8 "compromised" CAs is a single byte: https://mastodon.catgirl.cloud/@49016/117474217042191790

One of the private keys is literally "4".

I'm putting "compromised" in quotes here, because I can't call it that without cringing and cursing.

[cf. also: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50169109]

children.author: neya
children.textRawHtml: These clowns were responsible for getting a key as part of the process of getting an import/export license in India. It used to be a requirement to get a USB hardware key from them. India doesn't have any stringent data protection laws, so nothing will happen to them, even. None of their customers will actually even get to know about this incident unless they hear about it from elsewhere as most of the times, Indian companies never communicate such breaches to their customers (Eg. Domino's Pizza India had a massive breach and they never even sent as much as an email). It's really a sad state for privacy.

Basically no one outside the major browsers verifies CT logs, so you can still attack a lot of people even without publishing.

We wouldn’t.

CAs publish to CT logs. If an attacker has the private key, nothing stops them from signing certs without the involvement of the CA or CT logs.
